about: What someone of a kind of life is seen doing and says of their work, for the professions the portraits show that have no lines of their own (data/catalog/professions.json, and Orsino's backgrounds beyond the authored occupations): {Name} is the person, {trade} their profession by name, {them} and {their} by their pronouns. Read by Community when a settlement takes residents of such professions.

seen: {Name} the {trade} is scraping mud from {their} boots on the step, a brace of snared rabbits at {their} feet.
{Name} is sitting on a log by the door, mending a strap and watching the treeline.
{Name} the {trade} comes in from the fields with burrs on {their} sleeves.
talk: 'Follow the water downhill and you will come out somewhere,' says {Name}. 'That is the first thing a {trade} learns.'
'Three days without a roof,' says {Name}. 'You get to like it. Then it rains.'
'If you're going past the last field, go with the light behind you,' says {Name}. 'That's all a {trade} can tell you for free.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is checking the shoes of a tired horse, one hoof at a time.
{Name} is counting coins into a purse by the road, lips moving.
{Name} sits against the wall with {their} pack beside {them} and {their} boots off.
talk: 'Thirty years a {trade},' says {Name}. 'The roads are worse than they were, and the inns are dearer.'
'The ford's high and the bridge wants a toll,' says {Name}. 'Pick which you'd rather pay with: your feet or your purse.'
'People think a {trade} sees the world,' says {Name}. 'I see the road, and the back of a horse.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} has a brass lock in pieces on a cloth, a lens screwed into one eye.
{Name} is filing a blank key, trying it in a padlock after every few strokes.
{Name} has the back off a clock and is oiling its wheels with a feather.
talk: 'Everything made can be unmade by the one who knows how it was made,' says {Name}. 'That's the whole of being a {trade}.'
'Bring it to me if it sticks,' says {Name}. 'Don't force it. Forcing is what breaks things, and I charge more to mend broken.'
'Most locks fail at the spring,' says {Name}. 'Not the bolt.'

seen: {Name} leans in a dark doorway, watching who passes.
{Name} the {trade} is shuffling a worn pack of cards one-handed.
{Name} glances at your purse, then at your face, then away.
talk: 'I'm a {trade},' says {Name}, 'which is a respectable word for what I am.'
'Ask me nothing and I'll tell you nothing,' says {Name}. 'Ask me something and it'll cost you.'
'Everyone in this place owes somebody,' says {Name}. 'Knowing who, that's my living.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is grinding yarrow in a mortar, and the smell is sharp across the way.
{Name} is washing {their} hands in a basin until the water runs clear, and then again.
{Name} is binding a child's grazed knee on the step.
talk: 'Most of what I do is tell people to rest,' says {Name}. 'Most of what they do is not listen. That's a {trade}'s life.'
'Fever's going round the low houses,' says {Name}. 'Boil your water. Nobody does.'
'Bring me the wound early and I'll mend it,' says {Name}. 'Bring it me late and I'll pray with you.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is sweeping a doorstep, and blessing each corner of it in turn.
{Name} is reading the evening office from a small book, lips moving.
{Name} sits still by the door with {their} hands folded and {their} eyes closed.
talk: 'The gods ask very little,' says {Name}. 'It's the asking that's hard. I'm the {trade} here; I do the asking.'
'Come to the evening rite if you like,' says {Name}. 'It does no harm. It does a little good.'
'People come to a {trade} when they're frightened,' says {Name}. 'I'd sooner they came before.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is copying a page from a borrowed book, a stone on each corner.
{Name} is writing small and fast in a notebook, and covers the page with {their} sleeve when you come near.
{Name} is measuring the letters of a rubbing with a knotted string.
talk: 'Everything is written down somewhere,' says {Name}. 'Being a {trade} is knowing where.'
'Most of what is written in a town was written by its clerks,' says {Name}. 'Clerks lie in small, careful ways.'
'I came here for a month to read the stones by the river,' says {Name}. 'That was nine years ago.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is knocking dried clay from a pick, a careful blow at a time.
{Name} has grey dust to the elbows and a lantern hooked to {their} belt even in daylight.
{Name} is splitting a lump of slate with a chisel, looking at the grain.
talk: 'The ground keeps what you give it and gives back what it likes,' says {Name}. 'A {trade} learns not to argue.'
'There's good stone under the hill,' says {Name}. 'There's always good stone under the hill. Getting it out is the trouble.'
'Mind the old workings,' says {Name}. 'They don't hold up for anybody.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is running a stone along a blade in long, unhurried strokes.
{Name} stands by the door with a cudgel at {their} belt, watching the street.
{Name} is showing a boy how to hold a staff, and correcting his feet without a word.
talk: 'Every fight you walk away from is one you've won,' says {Name}. 'That's a {trade}'s whole wisdom, and nobody believes it till they're old.'
'If there's trouble on the road, I'm for hire,' says {Name}. 'If there isn't, I'm for a drink.'
'Keep your guard up and your mouth shut,' says {Name}. 'Most of what kills people is the second one.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is coiling a wet rope over {their} arm and elbow, neat as a skein.
{Name} smells of tar, and is watching the western sky for weather.
{Name} is mending a net with a wooden needle, quick as knitting.
talk: 'The water's up two hands since spring,' says {Name}. 'A {trade} watches the water. Nobody else does.'
'A still morning on the water means wind by noon,' says {Name}.
'I take people across when the water is low enough,' says {Name}. 'It is not, this week.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is saying lines under {their} breath, a playbook open on {their} knee.
{Name} is darning the hem of a red stage cloak.
{Name} is touching up a painted backcloth of a castle with a small brush.
talk: 'Give me a crowd and I'll give them a night,' says {Name}. 'That's what a {trade} is for.'
'They paid in turnips at the last place,' says {Name}. 'Good turnips. I'm not proud.'
'Everyone's a player,' says {Name}. 'Only some of us are paid for it, and not well.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is weighing a handful of nails on a small brass scale.
{Name} is reckoning the week's takings on a slate.
{Name} has an apron with a pocket for every tool and is mending a hinge, tapping the pin home with a small hammer.
talk: 'Everything has a price,' says {Name}. 'A {trade} only knows what it is first.'
'Business is poor,' says {Name}, 'which is what I say when it's good, so you'll not ask for credit.'
'I'll make it, mend it or buy it,' says {Name}. 'I won't explain it.'

seen: {Name} the {trade} is reading a letter with great attention and a seal broken on the table beside it.
{Name} crosses the way with a clerk behind {them} carrying {their} papers.
{Name} is dictating to a clerk who cannot write as fast as {they} can talk.
talk: 'There are rules for everything,' says {Name}. 'Being a {trade} means knowing which ones are true.'
'Petitions on the first day of the week,' says {Name}. 'Complaints on any other.'
'I hear everything that is said in this place,' says {Name}, 'eventually.'

seen: {Name} sits with {their} back to a warm wall and a bowl beside {them}, watching the feet go by.
{Name} the {trade} is sorting rags by colour into three small heaps.
{Name} is eating a heel of dry bread, slowly.
talk: 'Nobody looks at a {trade},' says {Name}. 'So I see everything.'
'I was somebody once,' says {Name}. 'Not much of a somebody. More than this.'
'A copper for a story,' says {Name}. 'A true one costs two.'
